l: house (Claus's house), The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: Claus's house is built during the night by the Knooks from logs he has prepared. It has a large room with a fireplace, table, bench, and cupboard, along with a smaller room containing a bed, stool, stand, and dried moss.

l: Spirit of Happiness, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: The Spirit of Happiness enters Claus's heart while he sleeps in the Valley. It drives out his terror, care, and misgivings so that he will no longer be clouded by anxiety.

l: brook, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: The brook provides Claus with pure drinking water. Its ripples playfully race and sing as they move through the Valley.

l: Knooks, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: The Knooks silently and skillfully build Claus's house while he sleeps. They later cut and stack wood for his fireplace, and Claus thanks them for their work and knowledge of human needs.

l: Fairies, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: The Fairies bring Claus skillets, pots, dishes, pans, cooking tools, wool clothing, and other comforts. They also provide warm blankets and clothing as his life in the Valley begins.

l: Ryls, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: The Ryls of the Field Flowers promise to supply Claus with food so that he will not need to plow the ground and destroy the flowers and grass. They subsequently provide milk, bread, honey, apples, grapes, and continuing food supplies.

l: Ak, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: Ak has spoken to the Ryls of the Field Flowers about Claus. Although Ak has no command over the field Ryls because he is not of the Forest, they are willing to favor Claus because Ak loves him.

l: field flowers, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: The field flowers grow throughout the Valley and are tended by the Ryls of the Field Flowers. Claus refuses to destroy them by plowing the earth and values their songs and beauty.

l: food supplies, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: The Ryls of the Field Flowers provide Claus with food supplies so he will not have to cultivate the ground. These supplies include fresh milk, bread, honey, apples, and grapes, and they remain available whenever he is hungry.

l: Happiness, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: Happiness fills the Laughing Valley and is expressed by the brook, daffodils, sunbeams, and other living things. Claus recognizes the Valley as a place of happiness, joy, peace, and good-will.

l: Claus's life in the Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, MANHOOD / 1. The Laughing Valley
s: Claus's life in the Laughing Valley begins with the favor and friendship of the immortals. His house, food, clothing, firewood, and other needs are supplied, allowing him to live peacefully while preparing to do good work.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
s: Claus befriends children throughout the countryside and brings comfort and happiness to those who welcome him, though he is refused entry to the palace of the Lord of Lerd and the castle of Baron Braun. When winter arrives, Claus worries that the cold and snow will keep him from seeing the children. While indoors, he carves a wooden cat modeled after Blinkie, creating his first toy. Blinkie's reactions amuse Claus and confirm his pleasure in the finished work.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
s: Claus travels through the Valley and the surrounding plain to visit villages and befriend children. He comforts poor, abused, crippled, ailing, and grieving people, but he is refused admission to the palace of the Lord of Lerd and the castle of Baron Braun. During the winter, he carves a wooden cat from a stick of wood and makes his first toy.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
s: Children in the villages welcome Claus as a playfellow, riding on his shoulders, nesting in his arms, and clinging to his knees. They have been much neglected by their parents, so Claus's attention makes them very happy. Claus worries that winter will prevent him from seeing them.

l: Jack Frost, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
s: Jack Frost visits Claus at night and boasts that he will nip many noses, ears, and toes. After Claus asks him to spare the children because they are tender and helpless, Jack promises not to pinch a child that night if he can resist the temptation.

l: Blinkie, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
s: Blinkie is a large cat given to Claus by Peter the Knook, and she sits beside the hearth while Claus stays indoors. She watches Claus carve a wooden cat, first reacting angrily to the image and then recognizing that it is made of wood. She resumes purring and gives Claus admiring glances.

l: toy cat, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
s: The first toy is a wooden cat that Claus carves from a stick of firewood during a long winter evening. He shapes it with a cat's head, body, haunches, tail, ears, eyes, and nose, modeling it after Blinkie. The completed toy pleases Claus and amuses him when Blinkie reacts to it.

l: winter, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
s: Winter approaches after the flowers, beetles, butterflies, and brook have changed with the season. Snow covers the Laughing Valley, and the cold keeps Claus indoors for many days. During this period, Claus grows weary of having little to do and begins carving wood.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. How Claus Made the First Toy
s: The Laughing Valley is where Claus lives and where snowflakes fall heavily when winter arrives. Its winter weather covers Claus's dwelling in white and makes it difficult for him to visit the children.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: Claus rescues Weekum from a snowdrift during a storm and gives him a wooden cat to keep. The Ryls help Claus color a second wooden cat to resemble a real cat, and the toy brings comfort to a sick girl. Inspired by Shiegra, Claus then carves and paints a wooden lioness. These events begin Claus's great work of making toys for children.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: Claus rescues Weekum from a snowdrift, warms and feeds him, and carries him home to his mother. He makes and colors wooden cats with help from the Ryls, gives one to a sick girl, and then carves and paints a wooden lioness after Shiegra's suggestion.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: The Laughing Valley is covered in snow during a fierce winter storm. Claus lives there, and after the wind moves north and the snow settles, he travels through the Valley to help others.

l: Blinkie, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: Blinkie is Claus's real cat. She hides under the table when the wind blows into the house, sits as a model while Claus paints the toy cat, appears offended by the attention given to it, and later becomes terrified when Shiegra snarls at her.

l: toy cat, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: The toy cat is a wooden imitation of a real cat. Weekum likes it because it does not run away, scratch, or bite, and a colored toy cat later comforts a sick girl by easing her fever and pain.

l: Weekum, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: Weekum is a little boy who becomes lost while walking to his auntie's house during a snowstorm. Claus finds and cares for him, and Weekum receives the wooden cat and takes it home to his mother.

l: Ryls, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: The Red, Green, Yellow, Black, and Blue Ryls visit Claus while he is carving a wooden cat. They bring paints and brushes made from the colors they use on flowers and plants, then help color the cat to resemble a real one.

l: colored toy-making, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: Claus begins making better wooden cats after deciding children will enjoy toys that cannot scratch or bite. With the Ryls' paints, he colors the cats' features and body to imitate real cats, beginning his great work of making toys.

l: sick girl, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: A sick girl lies on a wretched cot in a poor hut near the palace of the Lord of Lerd. Claus gives her a colored wooden cat, which brings her pleasure, quiets her fever, lessens her pain, and helps her fall asleep.

l: Shiegra, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: Shiegra is an old lioness who has loved Claus since his babyhood and visits him in the Laughing Valley despite her dislike of snow-drifts. She suggests that Claus make a lioness toy, admires the finished likeness, and returns toward her forest home after snarling at Blinkie.

l: wooden lioness, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: Claus carves a wooden lioness in Shiegra's likeness, including her fierce teeth, frowning lines, crouching body, and long tail. He paints it with the Ryls' colors, and Shiegra considers it skillfully made and likely to please children.

l: rescue of Weekum, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. How the Ryls Colored the Toys
s: During a snowstorm, Claus hears a cry of distress and finds Weekum buried in a snowdrift. He carries the child into his house, warms and feeds him, lets him sleep with the wooden cat, and returns him safely to his mother the next morning.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: In spring, Mayrie and her younger brother visit Claus in the Laughing Valley to ask for toy cats. When Claus shows Mayrie an image of the lioness Shiegra, both children become frightened and flee. Claus makes Mayrie a wooden cat and decides to model future toys on mild animals instead of fierce creatures. His toys become popular, and the immortals help supply him with wood, paints, brushes, and tools.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: After winter ends, the Laughing Valley becomes filled with joyous excitement, with the brook, grass, sun, and other natural features seeming lively and happy. Claus says that living in the Laughing Valley, where everything else laughs, makes him sing, laugh, and whistle.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Claus welcomes Mayrie and her younger brother, feeds them, and gives the boy his last ready-made toy cat. After frightening Mayrie with Shiegra's image, he makes her a wooden cat and decides to use mild animals as models for future toys. His toy-making becomes so popular that he turns his living room into a workshop, while the Knooks, Ryls, and Fairies supply materials and tools.

l: Mayrie, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Mayrie visits Claus with her younger brother because she wants a toy cat. She cries when Claus gives the only ready cat to her brother, becomes terrified by Shiegra's image, and later happily watches Claus carve and paint a cat for her.

l: Mayrie's younger brother, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Mayrie's younger brother accompanies her to Claus's house and echoes her request for a cat. He receives Claus's last ready-made toy cat but drops it while fleeing in fear from Shiegra's image.

l: Shiegra, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Shiegra is the lioness known to Claus, who is familiar with her and is not afraid of her. Claus realizes that children may view her as terrifying rather than friendly.

l: Shiegra's image, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Claus takes the image of Shiegra from his cupboard and offers it to Mayrie as a toy. Its fierce teeth and glaring eyes frighten both children, so Claus locks it back in the cupboard and decides not to use fierce creatures as toy models.

l: toy cats, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Claus's toy cats are popular with children. He gives one to Mayrie's younger brother, carries two to children in town, and later carves and paints another cat for Mayrie.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Claus's toy animals spread in fame to cottages on the plain and in the village, and no child who visits him goes away empty-handed. After Mayrie's reaction, he chooses squirrels, rabbits, deer, and lambkins as gentler models, and begins making wooden rabbits and lambs.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Children travel to Claus's house to obtain his wonderful toys, while Claus carries gifts to children who are sick or crippled. Their visits create a path from the plain to his cottage, and their pleasure makes Claus happy.

l: colored toy-making, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Claus's toy-making grows from carving cats into a larger enterprise producing rabbits, lambs, and other animal figures. The Knooks provide wood, the Ryls provide paints and brushes, and the Fairies bring tools, allowing Claus to work continuously in his workshop.

l: Mayrie's fright, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 4. How Little Mayrie Became Frightened
s: Mayrie's fright begins when she sees the fierce teeth and glaring eyes of Shiegra's image. Her terror causes her and her brother to flee, and it teaches Claus that children's toys should be mild and pleasant rather than fierce.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Claus gives in to Bessie Blithesome’s request for a toy and seeks advice from Necile and the Queen of the Fairies about whether rich children should receive his toys. The Queen declares that all children’s wishes and sufferings matter equally, so Claus decides to make toys for rich and poor alike. Claus creates the first dolly from clay in the likeness of Necile, then makes a baby dolly and a dressed image of Bessie. He gives the Bessie image dolly to Mayrie after she breaks her toy cat, making her very happy.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Claus promises Bessie Blithesome that he will make her a toy, then consults Necile and the Queen of the Fairies about whether he should give toys to rich children. He creates several clay dolls, including a toy nymph and an image of Bessie, and gives the Bessie image dolly to Mayrie.

l: Bessie Blithesome, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Bessie Blithesome visits Claus with an escort of men-at-arms and asks for a toy, explaining that she has none despite being a rich lord’s daughter. Claus gives her a clay nymph doll, which she loves and calls her baby.

l: Mayrie, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Mayrie comes to Claus crying because she has broken her toy cat by dropping it twice. Claus gives her the silk-robed Bessie image dolly, and Mayrie receives it with great joy.

l: Necile, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Necile listens to Claus’s concern about giving toys to rich children and says that riches are only like a gown that can be put on or removed, while children remain alike. Claus makes the first toy nymph in her likeness.

l: Queen Zurline, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: The Queen of the Fairies tells Claus that rich and poor children alike naturally long for pretty playthings and can suffer loneliness or enjoy happiness. She declares that it is his duty to make all children glad.

l: Fairies, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: The Fairies help Claus make the Bessie image dolly by bringing colored silks, laces, and golden threads for its clothing.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: The Laughing Valley is where Claus lives and where Bessie’s cavalcade arrives at his dwelling. After consulting Necile and the Queen of the Fairies, Claus returns to the Valley to make dolls.

l: toy nymph, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Claus forms the toy nymph from moist clay, bakes it in the sun until it becomes hard, and paints it to resemble Necile. He gives it to Bessie, who loves it and calls it a dolly.

l: Bessie image dolly, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Claus makes the Bessie image dolly from clay, bakes it over glowing coals, and dresses it in a lavender silk gown, lace collar, and pink silk shoes. He paints its face with Bessie’s brown eyes, golden hair, and rosy cheeks before giving it to Mayrie.

l: toy, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Bessie asks Claus for a toy because there are no toys in the world but his. Claus first promises her the next toy he makes, and the toy nymph becomes the gift that delights her.

l: riches, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Claus initially thinks riches provide enough comforts that rich children should not need his toys. Necile explains that riches are like a removable gown and do not change the child beneath them.

l: children's happiness, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: The Queen of the Fairies teaches Claus that rich children can be as lonely, unhappy, gay, and happy as poor children. Children’s happiness therefore should not depend on whether they live in palaces or cottages.

l: Claus's decision to make toys for all children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: After hearing Necile and the Queen of the Fairies, Claus decides that all children may claim his services, whether they are rich or poor. He then begins making toys for Bessie as well as for poor children.

l: creation of the first dolly, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: Claus unintentionally shapes moist clay into a head resembling Necile, then develops it into a toy nymph with hair, an oak-leaf gown, sandals, painted eyes, teeth, lips, and hair. The baked and painted figure becomes the first dolly, which he gives to Bessie.

l: Mayrie receiving the dolly, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 5. How Bessie Blithesome Came to the Laughing Valley
s: When Mayrie’s toy cat is broken, Claus offers her the silk-robed Bessie image dolly instead. Mayrie loves the beautiful figure and carries it home happily, saying it is better than cats.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The Awgwas are invisible, evil creatures who influence people toward wickedness and decide to destroy Claus because his toys make children happier and more obedient. They abduct Claus to a jungle in Ethop and later imprison him in a mountain cave, but the Knooks and Fairies rescue him, while Queen Zurline and other immortals protect his home. The Awgwas then steal Claus's toys and prevent children from reaching the Laughing Valley, causing Claus to stop traveling and fill his home with toys. Finally, Claus asks the great Ak for help against the Awgwas' persecution.

l: Awgwas, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The Awgwas are gigantic, evil creatures who are invisible to ordinary people but visible to immortals. They influence human minds, delight in wicked deeds, fight among themselves, and use their powers to attack Claus and prevent him from bringing happiness to children.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: Claus makes toys to bring happiness to children and thereby keeps them from the Awgwas' influence. After being abducted and repeatedly attacked, he continues making toys, but eventually asks the great Ak for help when the Awgwas prevent him from delivering them.

l: King Awgwa, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The King Awgwa proposes destroying Claus because Claus's toys have made children less naughty and less vulnerable to the Awgwas. He orders attempts to abduct, imprison, and rob Claus, but each effort to destroy or permanently confine him fails.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The children are influenced by the Awgwas to quarrel, disobey, and behave badly, but Claus's toys make them happier and more obedient. The Awgwas prevent them from finding the Laughing Valley after Claus stops traveling to the villages.

l: Knooks, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The Knooks of the Forest rescue Claus after the Awgwas leave him bound in the jungle of Ethop. Recognizing the secret sign and signal of their order, they free him, give him food and drink, and transport him back to the Laughing Valley.

l: Queen Zurline, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: Queen Zurline learns of Claus's persecution and declares that the immortals must protect him. She places her Seal on every door and window of Claus's dwelling, adding it to the Seals of the Fairies, Ryls, and Knooks.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The Laughing Valley is Claus's home and the place where he makes his toys. The Awgwas prevent children from reaching it after Claus gives up trying to travel to the villages.

l: immortals, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The immortals fear and avoid the Awgwas, although the Awgwas are visible to them. The immortals' friendship protects Claus: the Fairies rescue him from the mountain cave, and their Seals guard his dwelling.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The children's toys made by Claus bring happiness and encourage children to be obedient, reducing the Awgwas' influence over them. The Awgwas repeatedly steal the toys and store them in a lonely cavern, while Claus continues making more until his shelves are filled.

l: the Awgwas' wickedness, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The Awgwas' wickedness includes inspiring angry passions, encouraging children to eat unripe fruit and disobey their parents, and taking pleasure in their suffering and punishment. They also attack Claus because his work limits their power over children.

l: the Awgwas' plot against Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The Awgwas' plot is to remove Claus from the children by abducting him, imprisoning him, stealing his toys, and blocking children from reaching him. Their attempts fail to destroy Claus, but they succeed for a time in keeping him from delivering his toys.

l: Claus's abduction, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The Awgwas first bind the sleeping Claus and carry him to a remote jungle in Ethop, where they leave him among dangerous animals. Later, they seize him while he travels to a village and imprison him in a mountain cave behind huge rocks.

l: Claus's escape, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 6. The Wickedness of the Awgwas
s: The Knooks rescue Claus from the jungle after he uses their secret sign and signal, then transport him home to the Laughing Valley. When the Awgwas imprison him in a mountain cave, the Fairies answer his mystic words and carry him back home.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: Ak confronts the Awgwas after they persecute Claus, but their King refuses to stop and declares that Claus will be killed within three days. Ak gathers the immortals, who prepare for war against the Awgwas and the evil creatures summoned to support them. In the battle at Laughing Valley, the immortals defeat the Awgwas, Dragons, Goblins, and most of the Giants, allowing Claus to carry his toys safely to children. Ak explains that the Awgwas have perished and that the powers of Good cannot be overthrown when opposed to Evil.

l: Ak, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: Ak tells the Awgwas that Claus is under the protection of the immortals and orders them not to harm him. When the Awgwa King declares war and threatens to kill Claus, Ak organizes the immortals for battle, kills the King Awgwa with his ax, and later tells Claus that the Awgwas have perished.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: Claus is protected by the immortals after the Awgwas interfere with his work. While the battle is fought on his account, he remains in the Laughing Valley making toys, and afterward Ak tells him that he may carry them to children without fear.

l: Awgwas, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: The Awgwas refuse to stop persecuting Claus and defy Ak, claiming that their powers equal those of the immortals. They summon evil allies for war, but the immortals destroy them, turning them into earthen hillocks.

l: King Awgwa, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: The King Awgwa rejects Ak's demand to leave Claus unharmed and threatens to kill Claus within three days. He leads a large army against the immortals, but Ak cleaves him in two with his ax.

l: immortals, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: The immortals agree that the Awgwas must be destroyed because they devote themselves to evil and threaten Claus. They gather in the Laughing Valley and defeat the forces of evil before returning to their duties in the Forest.

l: war between the immortals and the spirits of evil, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: The war begins after the Awgwas refuse to obey Ak and threaten to kill Claus. The immortals fight the Awgwas and their allies in the Laughing Valley and win the battle.

l: spirits of evil, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: The spirits of evil are summoned by the King Awgwa to fight the immortals and include Asiatic Dragons, Tatary Giants, Black Demons, Goozzle-Goblins, and mountain Awgwas. Their forces are defeated, with only some of the Giants escaping.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: The Laughing Valley is where Claus makes his toys and where Ak orders the immortals to assemble for battle. The valley becomes the battlefield in which the immortals defeat the Awgwas and their allies.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: Claus continues making toys in the Laughing Valley while the immortals fight to protect him. After the Awgwas are destroyed, Ak tells Claus that he can carry the toys to dwellings and villages without fear.

l: Law, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: The Law states that Evil may accomplish terrible deeds when unopposed, but the powers of Good cannot be overthrown when opposed to Evil. The text says that the King Awgwa's ignorance of this Law costs him his existence.

l: Good, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: Good is represented by the immortals and their powers, which cannot be overthrown when they oppose Evil. The forces of Good defeat the Awgwas and their allies in the battle.

l: Evil, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 7. The Great Battle Between Good and Evil
s: Evil is represented by the Awgwas and the creatures they summon, whose actions are devoted to harm and misery. Evil is defeated when the immortals oppose it in battle.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Claus makes several journeys to distribute toys, then creates new dolls, animals, and musical instruments after studying children's tastes. During a deep winter, Flossie and Glossie visit him and help him build a sledge and harness so they can pull him to distant villages. On their first journey together, Claus travels by night, enters houses through chimneys, and leaves toys for sleeping children in a village and a large city. He empties his pack and barely returns to the Laughing Valley before daybreak, allowing the deer to reach the Forest before the Knooks' deadline.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Claus carries toys to children in hamlets, farmhouses, villages, and a large city, receiving grateful welcomes. He makes a sledge and harness, then rides with Flossie and Glossie on his first long journey with the reindeer, entering houses through chimneys to leave toys for sleeping children. He returns to the Laughing Valley just before daybreak.

l: Flossie, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Flossie visits Claus with Glossie and explains that the snow is frozen hard enough for deer to walk on. She obtains permission from Will Knook to draw Claus on a journey, helps pull his sledge through the night, and urges Claus to hurry when dawn approaches.

l: Glossie, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Glossie visits Claus with Flossie and explains that the Frost King has hardened the snow. He agrees to pull Claus's sledge after receiving permission from Will Knook, helps leap from roof to roof, and races back toward the Forest before daybreak.

l: Knooks, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: The Knooks are the guardians of Flossie and Glossie. Their permission is required for the deer to make the journey with Claus, and they would punish the deer if they failed to return to Burzee by daybreak.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: The Laughing Valley is Claus's home and workshop, where he stores and makes toys. Claus begins and ends his first journey with the reindeer there.

l: Forest, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: The Forest is where Claus had known Flossie and Glossie, and where the deer normally live under the guardianship of the Knooks. The deer must return to the Forest by daybreak after their journey.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Children everywhere receive toys from Claus, including children who have never owned a toy. During the first journey with the reindeer, sleeping children in villages and a city receive dolls, drums, horns, elephants, and other playthings.

l: reindeer, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: The reindeer can walk easily across deep snow when its surface is frozen hard, and their fleet feet allow them to travel much faster than Claus can walk. Flossie and Glossie pull Claus and his pack on a sledge, leap between rooftops, and race home before dawn.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Claus makes and distributes dolls, animal figures, drums, cymbals, whistles, and horns. He leaves toys for sleeping children during his journeys until his supply is exhausted.

l: sledge, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Claus constructs a rude sledge from material in his wood-pile, using two upward-curving runners and short boards for a platform. He places a stool and his pack of toys on it, and Flossie and Glossie pull it swiftly over the snow and across rooftops.

l: harness, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Claus makes a harness by twisting strong cords into collars for the deer and attaching other cords to the front of the sledge. He also uses cords fastened to the deer's antlers as reins, and later cuts the harness away so the deer can return to the Forest.

l: pack of toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Claus fills a pack with his prettiest toys and carries it on the sledge during the first journey with the reindeer. He empties the pack while visiting houses in a village and a large city.

l: snow, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: The Valley's snow lies many feet deep, but the Frost King freezes its surface so the deer can walk and the sledge can travel over it. The snow later supports the deer's rapid journey home, while Claus tumbles into a snowdrift when the sledge stops.

l: chimneys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Claus uses chimneys to enter houses whose doors are locked at night. He climbs down them to leave toys for sleeping children and climbs back up to return to the sledge.

l: villages, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: In a village Claus has never visited, he discovers that the locked doors prevent ordinary entry. With the deer's help, he reaches the rooftops, visits the houses through their chimneys, and leaves toys for every sleeping child.

l: the first journey with the reindeer, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: The first journey with the reindeer takes Claus, Flossie, and Glossie through the night to a village and a large city. Claus distributes his toys through chimneys and returns to the Laughing Valley just before daybreak, while the deer hurry back to the Forest.

l: colored toy-making, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 8. The First Journey with the Reindeer
s: Toy-making keeps Claus busy through the winter while deep snow prevents him from traveling. After observing children, he decides to make more dolls, animal figures, drums, cymbals, whistles, and horns.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 9. "Santa Claus!"
s: Claus's gifts become widely known, and people tell children stories about his wonderful toys. Parents explain that the toys came from the good Claus, whom mothers begin to regard as a Saint because of his mysterious ability to enter homes. Santa Claus brings toys because children are little and helpless and because he loves them, not because they are always well behaved. His good deeds cause people to enshrine him as a Saint in their hearts.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 9. "Santa Claus!"
s: Santa Claus becomes famous for giving wonderful toys to children. Mothers come to regard him as a Saint who can enter homes without unlocking doors, but he does not approve of using his gifts to threaten naughty children. He gives toys because children are little and helpless and because he loves them.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 9. "Santa Claus!"
s: Children find pretty toys by their bedsides and ask their parents where they came from. They are told that the good Claus brought them, and mothers teach them to pray to Santa Claus for forgiveness when they are naughty or disobedient. The text says that the best children are sometimes naughty and naughty children are often good.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 9. "Santa Claus!"
s: The toys Claus leaves by children's bedsides are described as pretty and wonderful. Parents say that they are the only toys in all the world made by the good Claus. Their appearance causes children and their parents to wonder how Claus entered the homes.

l: good deeds, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 9. "Santa Claus!"
s: Claus's generous work brings him fame that spreads into far lands, despite sneers from a few selfish people. His good deeds cause people to honor him as a Saint in their hearts.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Santa Claus asks Ak and other immortals to save Glossie and Flossie from punishment and secure permission for deer to draw his sledge on Christmas Eve. The Prince of the Knooks grants permission for up to ten deer to accompany Claus once a year, provided they return to the Forest by daybreak, and names them reindeer. Fairies recover the toys stolen by the Awgwas just before Christmas Eve, allowing Claus to make his first Christmas Eve journey and deliver gifts to children. He returns safely before daybreak, beginning a mission that brings happiness to hundreds of homes.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Santa Claus consults Ak after Will Knook threatens to punish Glossie and Flossie for returning one minute after daybreak. With the recovered toys, he makes his first Christmas Eve journey, delivering presents to children and returning home before daybreak.

l: Glossie, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Glossie helps Claus on his night journey and returns one minute after daybreak, nearly receiving punishment from Will Knook. Glossie says the trip was enjoyable and later carries Claus swiftly home before daybreak on Christmas Eve.

l: Flossie, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Flossie helps Claus on his night journey and returns one minute after daybreak, nearly receiving punishment from Will Knook. Flossie explains that they tried to get home by daybreak and later races with Glossie to return before dawn.

l: Will Knook, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Will Knook complains that Glossie and Flossie disobeyed his orders by staying out past daybreak and threatens to set stinging gnats on them. He objects to deer drawing Claus's sledge, but the Prince of the Knooks orders him to obey the granted permission.

l: Ak, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Ak hears Claus's account and summons the Prince of the Knooks, the Fairy Queen, and the Prince of the Ryls to consider the deer’s punishment and service. He persuades the immortals to support Claus and calls Glossie and Flossie to confirm that they willingly drew the sledge.

l: Prince of the Knooks, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The Prince of the Knooks grants Claus permission to use up to ten deer once each year on Christmas Eve. He requires the deer to return to the Forest by daybreak and names those serving Claus reindeer, granting them additional protections and benefits.

l: Fairy Queen, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The Fairy Queen promises that no harm will come to the deer while they are away from the Forest. At Ak's request, she also tries to find the toys stolen by the Awgwas and sends Fairies to search for them.

l: Awgwas, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The Awgwas hid Claus's stolen toys in a deep cave in the mountains and covered the entrance with rocks. Their hiding place is eventually discovered and opened by the Fairies.

l: Knooks, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The Knooks guard the deer in the Forest and are described as unaccustomed to granting favors. Their Prince ultimately allows selected deer to serve Claus on Christmas Eve.

l: Fairies, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The Fairies search the mountains for the toys stolen by the Awgwas. By joining hands and moving through the rocks from the peak downward, they discover the cave, open it, carry out the toys, and bring them to Claus.

l: reindeer, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The reindeer are deer permitted to draw Claus's sledge on Christmas Eve, with up to ten allowed each year. They receive access to nourishing and strengthening plants, the Pool of Nares, and the Fairy Queen's protection, provided they return by daybreak.

l: Forest, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The Forest is where the Knooks guard the deer and where Glossie and Flossie must return before daybreak. The deer serving Claus may bathe in its Pool of Nares.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The Laughing Valley is where Claus returns to work after consulting Ak. He leaves it with Glossie and Flossie at moonrise for his Christmas Eve journey and returns there after distributing the toys.

l: sledge, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Claus's sledge is drawn by Glossie and Flossie during his first Christmas Eve journey. Claus repairs its harness and strengthens it before loading it with toys and traveling south.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The Awgwas had stolen Claus's toys and hidden them in a cave beneath rocks in the mountains. The Fairies recover the toys just in time for Claus to load them onto his sledge and give them to children.

l: Christmas Eve, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Christmas Eve is established as the one night each year when Claus may use up to ten deer to draw his sledge. Claus's first journey on Christmas Eve takes him to farmhouses and a village, where he leaves toys for sleeping children.

l: Claus's first Christmas Eve journey, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Claus's first Christmas Eve journey begins after the Fairies recover the stolen toys. He travels with Glossie and Flossie, distributes gifts at farmhouses and in a village, empties his sack, and returns before daybreak.

l: recovery of the stolen toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: The recovery of the stolen toys occurs when the Fairies search through the mountain in a joined line and find the cave where the Awgwas hid them. They break open the cave and carry the toys to Claus shortly before Christmas Eve.

l: Santa Claus's mission to bring happiness to children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 10. Christmas Eve
s: Santa Claus's mission to bring happiness to children begins with his first Christmas Eve delivery of toys to sleeping children. The text says he has continued this mission for hundreds of years, bringing happiness to children's hearts.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: Santa Claus builds a larger sledge and prepares a team of ten reindeer so he can carry more toys to children on Christmas Eve. With help from the Gnome King and Peter Knook, he obtains steel runners, sleigh-bells, and strong leather harness materials. On one Christmas Eve, Margot, Dick, Ned, and Sara hang their wet stockings by the chimney, and Santa Claus fills them with toys. The children tell others, beginning the tradition of hanging stockings for Santa Claus, which helps him deliver presents more quickly.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: Santa Claus decides to spend the year making toys and to deliver them to children on Christmas Eve. He builds a larger sledge, obtains a harness for ten reindeer, and improves his toys with suggestions from the immortals. He fills the stockings of Margot, Dick, Ned, and Sara when he sees them hanging by the chimney.

l: reindeer (Claus's reindeer), The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: Santa Claus's ten reindeer consist of Glossie, Flossie, Racer, Pacer, Reckless, Speckless, Fearless, Peerless, Ready, and Steady. They are selected for their likeness to Glossie and Flossie, strengthened with the casa plant, made fleet with the grawle plant, and given long lives through the marbon plant. They wear a new leather harness and pull Santa Claus's large sledge swiftly through the night.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: Children receive Santa Claus's toys and speak of him with love because of his unselfish deeds. Margot, Dick, Ned, and Sara discover toys in their stockings and tell their friends about it. Other children then decide to hang their stockings by the fireplace on Christmas Eve.

l: Santa Claus's new sledge, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: Santa Claus's new sledge is larger, stronger, and better suited for swift travel than his old one. It has curled steel runners from the Gnome King, a high rounded dashboard, high sides, and enough room for three full sacks of toys and additional toys in the sledge-box. The deer first consider it too large and heavy for two of them, so Santa Claus uses a team of ten.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: Santa Claus's toys become more beautiful and attractive as he works on them throughout the year. Some dolls say "papa" and "mama," lambs squeak, birds whistle, horses have wheels, and one donkey has a nodding head. On Christmas Eve, he loads three sacks and the rest of the sledge with toys for children.

l: the first stockings tradition, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: The first stockings tradition begins when Margot, Dick, Ned, and Sara's wet stockings are hung by the chimney to dry. Santa Claus notices them, fills them with toys, and inspires the children to tell others about what happened. The custom spreads, helping Santa Claus find children and deliver their presents more quickly.

l: Christmas Eve, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: On Christmas Eve, Santa Claus travels with his ten reindeer and a large load of toys to visit children around the world. The first stockings are hung by the chimney on this night, and Santa Claus fills them during his hurried visit. In later years, children hang stockings in anticipation of his arrival.

l: Santa Claus's Christmas-night journey, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: Santa Claus's Christmas-night journey takes him swiftly from chimney to chimney in his new sledge. He uses ten reindeer and sings as they travel over the frozen snow. After discovering the children's stockings, he realizes that filling them saves time compared with finding each child and placing toys beside the bed.

l: stockings (children's stockings), The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 11. How the First Stockings Were Hung by the Chimneys
s: The children's stockings are hung in a row by the chimney so they can dry after Margot, Dick, Ned, and Sara play in the snow. Santa Claus sees them, stuffs toys into them, and leaves the children delighted the next morning. Their use spreads among other children as a convenient way for Santa Claus to deliver presents.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 12. The First Christmas Tree
s: Claus continues traveling around the world each Christmas Eve, bringing toys, fruit, candies, and other gifts to children. He discovers the idea of decorating a tree when he visits three neglected children living beneath a tent on a treeless plain. The children and their parents are filled with wonder, and Claus later carries Christmas trees to poor homes and decorates them with candles and toys. Years later, the new Baron Braun respectfully asks Claus to visit his children, and Claus agrees.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 12. The First Christmas Tree
s: Claus travels over the world on his sledge and returns to the Laughing Valley by daybreak. He brings children toys, fruit, candies, and decorated trees, and his kindness wins the hearts of everyone. He visits the children of the new Baron Braun after the Baron humbly asks him to do so.

l: reindeer (Claus's reindeer), The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 12. The First Christmas Tree
s: Claus's ten reindeer carry him swiftly on his yearly trips around the world. Over eight years, each reindeer receives a string of bells from the Gnome King, so that all ten wear bells and make a merry tune as the sledge travels.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 12. The First Christmas Tree
s: Children receive toys, oranges, bananas, candies, and bonbons from Claus in their long stockings. They look forward to his yearly visit and gain happiness by wondering what will happen when he arrives. The children of the new Baron Braun long for a visit from Santa Claus, and Claus promises to bring them presents.

l: three little children (beneath the tent), The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 12. The First Christmas Tree
s: The three little children live beneath a rude tent of skins on a broad treeless plain, and their parents sadly neglect them. Claus plants a pine tree near their tent, decorates it with candles, toys, and candies, and gives them their first great pleasure. They dance and laugh around the sparkling tree, while their parents begin to show them more respect and consideration.

l: pine tree (the tree Claus planted), The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 12. The First Christmas Tree
s: Claus picks up the bushy top of a pine tree that the wind has broken off and carries it in his sledge. He plants it in the sand before the tent of the three little children and decorates its branches with candles and toys.

l: Christmas tree, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 12. The First Christmas Tree
s: The first Christmas tree in this account is made when Claus plants a pine tree for the three little children and decorates it with candles, toys, and candies. Pleased with the idea, Claus later carries trees to poor homes and decorates them for the children, while some fathers obtain trees for him to prepare.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: Santa Claus grows old and weak after many years of making and delivering toys to children, and the Forest of Burzee and Laughing Valley mourn his approaching death. Necile asks Ak for help, so he summons a council of the immortals to decide whether Claus deserves the Mantle of Immortality. Every immortal votes yes, and the Mantle is brought from its crypt and bestowed upon Claus. The Mantle becomes part of Claus's being, driving away the Spirit of Death and making him immortal.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: Santa Claus grows old, with white hair and beard, wrinkles, and a stout, waddling form, but he remains lively, jolly, and kind. After his strength is exhausted and he stops making toys, the immortals bestow the Mantle of Immortality upon him, making it part of his being.

l: Necile, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: Necile, who reared Santa Claus as his foster mother, remains youthful, strong, and beautiful while he grows old. Troubled by the fate threatening Claus, she seeks Ak's help and later kisses Claus while admiring his immortal form.

l: Ak, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: Ak summons a council of the immortals after Necile tells him that Claus is near death. He argues that Claus deserves immortality and persuades the council to bestow the Mantle of Immortality upon him.

l: Spirit of Death, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: The Spirit of Death hovers near Santa Claus's bedside. When she sees the Mantle of Immortality, she retreats with disappointment and leaves the house forever.

l: Burzee, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: The Forest of Burzee becomes sad when Santa Claus grows old and appears near death. It later hosts the council where the rulers of the immortals gather to decide Claus's fate.

l: Laughing Valley, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: The Laughing Valley is described as a peaceful place where Santa Claus has lived and maintained perfect health for many years. When he grows old and weak, the Valley is hushed and mournful.

l: immortals, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: The immortals gather in Burzee to consider Santa Claus's claim to immortality. Every immortal votes to give him the Mantle, and they carry it from its crypt and bestow it upon him.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: Children are the recipients of Santa Claus's toys and the beneficiaries of his lifelong work. Ak argues that Claus should live on because children would miss and grieve over his loss.

l: Mantle of Immortality, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: The Mantle of Immortality is a unique robe that has existed since the Beginning and is kept in a gleaming crypt between earth and sky. After every immortal votes for its use, it is placed upon Santa Claus, sinks into his body, and becomes a permanent part of his being.

l: council of the immortals, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: The council of the immortals is summoned by Ak in the Forest of Burzee to decide whether Santa Claus should receive the Mantle of Immortality. All members vote yes.

l: immortality, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: Immortality is presented as a gift reserved for one who truly deserves it, and no mortal had previously claimed the Mantle. Santa Claus receives immortality because of his noble nature and lifelong service to children.

l: Santa Claus's mission to bring happiness to children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, OLD AGE / 1. The Mantle of Immortality
s: Santa Claus's Christmas work consists of making toys and distributing them to children throughout the world. He performs this work for many years with the assistance and goodwill of the immortals, until old age finally prevents him from making more toys.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: Santa Claus regains his youthful strength after winning the Mantle of Immortality through his love for little children. As the world’s population grows and spreads across the earth, Santa Claus expands his toy-making and gift-giving work with help from several immortals. Ak, the Knook Prince, the Ryl Prince, and the Fairy Queen each provide an assistant to help Santa Claus. Santa Claus’s reindeer carry him across land and sea so that he can visit children around the world each Christmas Eve.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: Santa Claus awakens with his old strength renewed and feels as vigorous and merry as a boy of sixteen, although his beard remains white and wrinkles remain around his eyes. After learning about the Mantle of Immortality, he prepares more toys than ever and resolves that no child, poor or rich, should go without a Christmas gift if he can provide one. As the number of children grows, he receives help from Kilter, Peter, Nuter, and Wisk and continues his yearly work across the world.

l: Ak, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: Ak tells Santa Claus about the Mantle of Immortality and explains that Santa Claus won it through his love for little children. He gives Santa Claus his man Kilter, known as 'the silent and swift,' to help with the work. Ak explains that he guarded the forests until people needed them and hopes that they will not cut down every tree.

l: Mantle of Immortality, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: The Mantle of Immortality was won by Santa Claus through his loving deeds toward little children. It restores his vigor and means that he need never fear being parted from his dear ones.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: Little children are loved by Santa Claus, whose devotion to them earns him the Mantle of Immortality. Their growing numbers increase Santa Claus’s work, and children throughout the world come to love him for the gifts and happiness he provides.

l: the World, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: The world grows older as generations pass, while its population increases and spreads into new lands. Forests are cleared for cities, fields, and cattle, and people cross oceans to build cities in far countries.

l: humanity, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: People become more numerous over the generations and spread across the earth in search of new homes. They cut down forests, build cities and fields, make ships from tree trunks, and cross oceans to settle in distant lands.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: Santa Claus decides that no child, poor or rich, should go without a Christmas gift if he can manage to supply one. The growing number of children requires him to prepare larger yearly loads of gifts.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: Santa Claus fashions new toys and begins making them in larger quantities as more children are born and spread across the world. Kilter, Peter, Nuter, and Wisk help him make the toys and prepare his yearly load.

l: Santa Claus's yearly journeys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 2. When the World Grew Old
s: Santa Claus’s yearly journeys extend farther as children spread over the earth. His reindeer travel over oceans as swiftly as over land, allowing his sledge to follow the sun and giving him twenty-four hours to encircle the earth each Christmas Eve.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Santa Claus discovers that new houses increasingly have narrow chimneys connected to stoves rather than fireplaces, preventing him from reaching the children inside. Kilter, Wisk, Peter, and Nuter propose entering through walls, and the four little folk accompany Santa Claus to distribute toys. Santa Claus later makes loving parents his deputies by asking them to prepare trees and stockings, while toy-shops supply additional gifts. Despite the growing number of children, Santa Claus remains committed to making them happy.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Santa Claus struggles to deliver toys when new-fashioned chimneys lead to stoves instead of fireplaces. He brings Kilter, Wisk, Peter, and Nuter with him so they can enter houses through the walls, and later asks loving parents to help distribute presents as his deputies. He also sends large supplies of toys to toy-shops so that children who are missed, ill, or celebrating birthdays can receive gifts.

l: Kilter, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Kilter gathers the notes and letters that children write to Santa Claus. He explains that he can pass through walls, and he joins Santa Claus on the Christmas journey to help distribute toys.

l: Wisk, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Wisk suggests that the little folk enter houses through walls when chimneys cannot be used. During the journey, he mischievously tickles the reindeer with a feather, so Santa Claus watches him and tweaks his ears to make him behave.

l: the four little folk, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: The four little folk, Kilter, Wisk, Peter, and Nuter, begin riding in Santa Claus's sledge and entering houses through walls. Their work helps Santa Claus distribute gifts more quickly, and they continue accompanying him on his yearly ride.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Children suffer disappointment when new houses prevent Santa Claus from reaching them. Santa Claus and his helpers work to ensure that children receive toys, including through parents and toy-shops, and Santa Claus says that no child should long for toys in vain if he can help it.

l: parents (of the children), The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: At first, some parents build houses that prevent Santa Claus from entering through fireplaces. Later, parents become anxious for Santa Claus to visit and are asked to prepare Christmas trees or hang up stockings; loving parents may fill them after Santa Claus leaves.

l: deputies of Santa Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: The deputies are the loving parents whom Santa Claus asks to help with his work. They prepare trees and stockings and may place the gifts in them after Santa Claus has departed.

l: chimneys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: New-fashioned chimneys are built narrow and may end in a cellar without a fireplace. Santa Claus initially tries to use them but nearly becomes stuck, and he later abandons them when he learns that they serve stoves.

l: stove, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Stoves are newly invented and increasingly used in houses in place of fireplaces. Their presence explains why some chimneys do not provide Santa Claus with an entrance into the house.

l: house, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: The new houses have narrow chimneys and stoves rather than the fireplaces Santa Claus expects. Santa Claus and the four little folk eventually enter such houses through the walls.

l: toys, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Santa Claus is unable to give away some toys when narrow chimneys block access to children. He later distributes toys with help from the four little folk, parents, and toy-shops.

l: toy-shops, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Santa Claus sends great heaps of toys to toy-shops. They provide gifts for children who are missed by Santa Claus, become ill, or need presents for birthdays.

l: Christmas Eve, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: On Christmas Eve, Santa Claus travels in his sledge to deliver gifts. The four little folk join him on this yearly journey and help him finish his work before daybreak.

l: children's happiness, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus, 3. The Deputies of Santa Claus
s: Santa Claus treats children's happiness as more important than the wishes or indifference of thoughtless parents. He works with helpers, parents, and toy-shops so that children can receive gifts and remain happy.

l: The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: This document tells the life and work of Claus, later known as Santa Claus, from his childhood in the Forest of Burzee through his becoming immortal and expanding his gift-giving across the world. Burzee is an ancient, uncivilized forest inhabited by immortal Fairies, Knooks, Ryls, Nymphs, and other beings. Necile, a wood-nymph, finds purpose when she defies the Forest Law to take in an abandoned human infant. Ak, the Master Woodsman, permits the adoption, protects the child, and names him Claus. Raised lovingly by Necile and the forest people, Claus grows up believing Burzee is the whole world. Ak eventually shows Claus humanity: its many people, unequal conditions, mortality, and especially its children. Moved by his own rescue as an infant, Claus leaves Burzee to help children and settles in the Laughing Valley of Hohaho. Supported by the immortals, he builds a home and begins making toys. Wooden cats, colored animals, dolls, and other creations bring comfort and joy to children. He learns that rich and poor children alike deserve care, and increasingly devotes himself to all of them. The invisible, wicked Awgwas see Claus’s happiness-making work as a threat. They kidnap him, steal his toys, and keep children away from him, but Ak and the immortals wage a battle in the Laughing Valley and defeat the Awgwas and their allies. Claus can then resume delivering toys. With the deer Flossie and Glossie, he creates a sledge and begins traveling by night, entering homes through chimneys and leaving toys for sleeping children. People come to call him Santa Claus and regard him as a Saint because he gives from love for little and helpless children. Christmas Eve journeys, reindeer, stockings by chimneys, and decorated Christmas trees arise through his work. After many years, Santa Claus becomes old, but Necile appeals to Ak and the immortals unanimously grant him the Mantle of Immortality. Renewed, he continues serving a growing world. As travel and access become harder, immortals assist him, reindeer carry him over land and sea, and Kilter, Wisk, Peter, and Nuter help him enter modern houses. Finally, Santa Claus makes loving parents his deputies, with trees, stockings, and toy-shops helping ensure that children continue to receive happiness.

l: Burzee, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Burzee is a mighty, grand, ancient forest, flourishing for hundreds of years and largely unreached by civilization or the human race. Its close-standing trees have big trunks, rough bark, gnarled limbs, bushy foliage roofing the forest, and intertwining roots and branches; sunbeams enter in little spots, while silence is generally unbroken. Nature peopled it in the beginning, and it is inhabited by nymphs and wood-nymphs, Fairies, Knooks, Ryls, animals, and other immortals. It is home to Fairies, Nymphs, and Necile, refuge for Knooks, and playground for Ryls, with the Laughing Valley of Hohaho at its eastern edge. Governed by the Law of the Forest, it has old, sturdy trees no longer threatened by weeds and Gadgols. Necile brings an infant there to raise safely; that child, Claus, grows up among its immortals and regards Burzee as the whole world. He explores its heart, learns natural lore, and helps maintain its plants and animals. After traveling around the world with Ak, Claus returns to the circle of nymphs, then leaves Burzee through its eastern edge to live among men. In his old age, when Santa Claus seems near death, Burzee becomes sad and hosts the council of immortal rulers who decide his fate.

l: Fairies, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Fairies are immortal, powerful guardians of mankind who protect humanity unseen, governed by laws forbidding familiarity with their human charges. Just and impartial, they nevertheless aid Claus when mystic words summon them, supplying warm clothing, blankets, household and work tools, and silks, laces, and golden threads for the Bessie image dolly. Later, when the Awgwas steal toys, the Fairies search the mountains, pass through rocks, find and open the cave, recover the toys, and carry them back to Claus.

l: Knooks, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: The Knooks are queer, crooked, ill-natured immortal forest beings who watch over gentle and wild beasts, keep animal order with Claus’s help, and enforce laws obeyed by many beasts. Skillful and silent, they build Claus’s house while he sleeps, then select, cut, and stack soft wood for his work and fireplace because they understand human needs. After Claus gives their secret sign, the Knooks of the Forest rescue him from the jungle of Ethop, feed him, and return him to the Laughing Valley. They guard the reindeer Flossie and Glossie, require permission for their journey with Claus, and threaten punishment if they do not return to Burzee by daybreak. Though reluctant to grant favors, their Prince permits selected deer to serve Claus on Christmas Eve.

l: Ryls, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Ryls are merry, light-hearted immortals, first cousins to the wood-nymphs, who watch over and tend flowers and plants as sacred work and are armed with sharp thorns. With Claus’s help, they promise him seasonal food, milk, bread, honey, apples, and grapes, so he need not plow and harm flowers or grass. Later, the Red, Green, Yellow, Black, and Blue Ryls bring paints and brushes, color a wooden cat, support colored toy-making, and add their seal to Claus’s protection.

l: Nymphs, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Nymphs are a forest people and immortal creatures: fair, youthful, innocent, pure, loving, dainty, and unchanging, with no need to regard time. They live happily in the Forest of Burzee, wear oak-leaf green, guard forests and trees, minister to young trees, and explain Burzee’s mysteries, habits, and living things. Sheltered in Burzee’s inner parts by its law, they dance at the Royal Circle each full moon and observe seasonal festivals and ceremonies. Queen Zurline is their queen, and they listen to Ak’s wisdom and serve Claus when called upon. They are dismayed by Necile and the infant at first, then support Ak’s permission for her to keep Claus, help find milk, and care for him. As Claus grows, they guide and protect him; when he leaves, they promise sympathy and help.

l: inhabitants of Burzee, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Burzee’s inhabitants, Fairies, Knooks, Ryls, and Nymphs, are sweet immortals placed by Nature, living, reveling, and playing undisturbed in the forest’s depths.

l: Civilization, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: has_reached Forest of Burzee [never yet] Civilization has never reached the Forest of Burzee. Whether it will ever reach the forest remains uncertain.

l: Necile, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Necile is a beautiful, immortal wood- and forest-nymph of the Forest of Burzee, closely related to Queen Zurline. With chestnut-bur-lined hair, eyes blue in sunlight and purple in shade, and an oak-leaf-green costume, she is highly regarded for beauty and grace. She lives in her bower, guards and waters the trees, keeps hurtful weeds away, and frightens Gadgols. As the forest becomes established and her duties lessen, she broods over her life, grows discontented, and longs for adventure, though the Law of the Forest restrains her from leaving. Hearing of a forsaken human infant in danger, Necile feels tender pity and wilfully defies that Law. She rescues the child at the forest's edge, brings him into Burzee, and asks Ak to allow her to keep and care for him. Once granted permission, she rejoices, names him Claus rather than Neclaus, prepares a moss bed, and raises him in her bower. She teaches him to speak, walk, play, and understand the forest and its inhabitants, adapting her life to follow him through Burzee. Her love becomes that of a devoted foster-mother: she weeps when Ak takes him away, anxiously awaits him, and grieves at his increasing thoughtfulness. When Claus leaves the forest, he remembers her as his loving foster-mother and comrade, promising to love and cherish her; she embraces and kisses him tenderly. She later speaks with him about children and riches, and he makes the first toy nymph in her likeness. While Santa Claus grows old, Necile remains youthful, strong, and beautiful. Troubled by the fate threatening him, she seeks Ak's help and finally admires and kisses his immortal form.

l: Queen Zurline, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Queen Zurline is a Fairy, Queen of the Wood-Nymphs, and lovely ruler of the Pool of Nares. She supports Necile's petition to keep an infant, tells Claus that all children deserve happiness and that he must make them glad, and guards children by advising him. When the Awgwas persecute Claus, she leads the immortals' protection by sealing his dwelling.

l: Ak, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Ak is the immortal Master Woodsman of the World: wise, farseeing, grizzled-bearded, and armed with a gleaming ax. He sees everything, knows more than mortals, makes and enforces the Law, and rules or oversees forests, orchards, and groves throughout the world. He guards Burzee, the Great Black Forest, and the wooded wilderness of Braz, while acknowledging that people will clear forests for settlement. He loves the wood-nymphs as a father loves children and sometimes aids helpless human children. Ak’s central concern becomes Claus. He rescues or protects endangered infants, including the newborn whom Necile takes despite his Law. Discovering her with the child, Ak relaxes the Law for the first and final time, permits the adoption, promises protection, and decrees that beasts and reptiles must not molest Claus. As Claus grows, Ak examines him, finds him brave and innocent, and becomes his master, teacher, guide, and friend. He takes Claus through the world, teaches him about mortals, unequal childhoods, his own babyhood, and the purpose of helpful lives, then returns him safely to Burzee. Ak continues to secure Claus’s work and safety. He wins the favor of the field Ryls, declares Claus protected by the immortals, organizes the immortals against the Awgwas, kills their king with his ax, and announces their defeat. When questions arise about the deer that draw Claus’s sledge, Ak gathers leading immortals, hears confirmation that Glossie and Flossie serve willingly, and persuades the immortals to support Claus. In Claus’s old age, Ak convenes the council after learning he is near death, argues that his love for little children merits immortality, and persuades the council to grant the Mantle of Immortality. He then explains this gift to Santa Claus and provides Kilter, the silent and swift, to help him continue his work.

l: Law of the Forest, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: The Law of the Forest keeps wood-nymphs in the forest; Necile knowingly breaks it to find a human infant.

l: humanity, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Humanity is a numerous, diverse group of mortals, born into wealth or poverty and varied conditions and occupations. Its members live brief lives of toil, worry, aging, and death, yet each has a mission to leave the world better than it was found. Over generations, humanity increases and spreads across the earth seeking new homes. It clears forests, builds cities, fields, and pasture, makes ships from tree trunks, crosses oceans, and settles distant lands. Claus recognizes this lot, accepts it as his own, and leaves the Forest to join humanity's struggle. Ak teaches that helpful people are sure to live again.

l: children, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Children are tender, helpless beings found in the city of men across sharply different conditions of wealth and poverty, though equally fair and sweet as babes. Often neglected by their parents, they welcome Claus as a playfellow, finding happiness in his attention and fearing winter will keep him away. Claus sees ragged children playing in dust and richly dressed children eating sugar-plums; their shared sweetness awakens his love, pity, and wish to help, because childhood seems the most contented time before humanity's cares arrive. They love toys and Santa Claus, receive his gifts in long stockings, and eagerly anticipate his yearly visits, including the children of Baron Braun. As their numbers grow worldwide, they become the purpose of Santa Claus's lifelong work and a reason he is granted immortality: they would grieve if he were lost. When obstacles such as new houses block his visits, he and his helpers seek other ways, through parents and toy-shops, to ensure no child longs for toys in vain.

l: Shiegra, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Shiegra is an old, formerly fierce lioness from the Forest of Burzee and Claus’s friend. She first crouches near an abandoned human infant intending to devour it, but Ak orders her to nurse and protect the child from every beast and reptile. She comes to love Claus from his babyhood and later visits him in the Laughing Valley despite the snow. She proposes a lioness toy, admires Claus’s wooden likeness of her, snarls at Blinkie, and returns toward her forest home. Though Claus trusts her, he recognizes that children may find her frightening.

l: Claus, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus
s: Claus is a human child, later known as Santa Claus, whose life is devoted to making children happy. Found newborn, abandoned, helpless, and crying near the Forest of Burzee, he is rescued by Necile, fed and protected by Shiegra and the forest people, and adopted as Necile's foster child. Raised among nymphs, Ryls, Knooks, Fairies, and Ak, he grows gentle, brave, innocent, and happy, learning their ways and believing the Forest is his whole world. As a strong youth, Claus helps the Forest people and journeys through the world with Ak. There he discovers that he is human and sees the suffering of humanity's children. Thoughtful after this journey, he leaves the Forest to live among people, while retaining the immortals' protection and aid. In the Laughing Valley, he builds a house from fallen trees, refuses to harm living trees, befriends children, and seeks to comfort those who are poor, sick, grieving, or helpless. During winter he makes a wooden cat, his first toy. With materials, colors, tools, and protection from his immortal friends, he becomes a skilled toy-maker, creating animals, dolls, and musical toys and giving them to children. Even attacks by the Awgwas do not turn him from this purpose. To reach more children, he builds a sledge and harness, guides reindeer, enters homes through chimneys, and delivers toys at night, returning to the Laughing Valley by daybreak. His yearly Christmas Eve journeys expand: he fills stockings, brings trees and gifts, and becomes beloved by children and honored as a Saint. In old age, Claus remains jolly and kind despite failing strength. Because of his love for little children, the immortals grant him the Mantle of Immortality, renewing his strength and giving him everlasting life.
